analysis.one_liner: Restores consumer-protection offices, staffing, and complaint transparency at the CFPB.
analysis.headline: The Consumers First Act was introduced in late September 2018 with six Democratic sponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a markup or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was written to push back on how the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the federal watchdog for mortgages, credit cards, payday loans, and debt collection, was being run after its director resigned in 2017. It would require the agency to keep its enforcement offices fully staffed, cap the number of political appointees, restore public access to its consumer complaint database, protect the Office of Fair Lending and the Office of Students and Young Consumers from being dismantled or renamed, and require an investigation into whether the new leadership suppressed a report about banks overcharging students on campus.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers: borrowers, credit card users, servicemembers protected by the Military Lending Act, students and their families, and seniors. A fully staffed, enforcement-focused CFPB means more scrutiny of hidden fees, discriminatory lending, abusive debt collection, and payday loan practices, and a public database where people can see which companies have complaints against them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers, students, servicemembers, and credit users

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFPB Director to give enforcement and supervision offices sufficient staff to do their jobs, and blocks the Director from reorganizing or renaming those offices [S3].
Restores the Office of Fair Lending's duty to actually implement enforcement and supervision of fair lending laws, which the bill says had been stripped away [S3].

Requires an Office of Students and Young Consumers led by a student loan ombudsman, and restores memoranda of understanding with the Department of Education so the two agencies can share information about student lending [S3].
Requires the agency to make its consumer complaint database fully public, searchable by company, linked from its home page, and available in multiple languages and accessible formats [S3].

Limits the number of political appointees at the agency to levels comparable to other financial regulators, and requires the Director to attend Consumer Advisory Board meetings and restores members dismissed from the board [S3].
Orders the Director to hand over records related to the student loan ombudsman's resignation, including whether leadership suppressed a campus banking report [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, student loan servicers, and other financial companies the CFPB regulates, who would face restored supervision, enforcement, and public complaint records, with some compliance costs potentially passed on to customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, loan servicers

drawbacks.text: The bill locks specific offices, boards, and even the agency's name into statute, limiting whatever director holds the job from restructuring the agency; critics of the agency have long argued it lacks accountability and that mandated structure prevents efficiency [S3].

Expanded supervision and enforcement raises compliance costs for lenders and servicers, which can be passed to consumers through fees or reduced access to credit; the bill also mandates extensive new reporting on offices, staffing, and interagency agreements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a consumer watchdog that actually enforces consumer financial law — directly affects people's mortgages, credit cards, and loans, and the transparency provisions cost taxpayers little. The main honest cost is reduced flexibility for the agency's leadership and higher compliance costs for regulated firms, some of which could reach consumers. On balance the bill's purpose is explicit in its text: to reverse a deliberate scaling back of consumer enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the final months of a Congress where Republicans controlled the House, it was referred to two committees and never came up for a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on September 28, 2018 with five Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the Financial Services and Education and the Workforce committees [S1].

The bill's own findings recount that after Director Richard Cordray resigned in November 2017, the White House installed the budget director as acting head of the agency, which it describes as dropping lawsuits against payday lenders, stopping payments of collected penalties to harmed consumers, cutting the agency's budget, and stripping enforcement powers from the fair lending office [S3].
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral [S5].
The 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, and the bill was not reintroduced action or carried forward in this session [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The financial firms that faced lighter CFPB supervision and enforcement in 2018 came out ahead; the agency's reduced posture under its acting leadership remained in place through the end of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms facing lighter consumer-agency oversight

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Consumers First Act to require the CFPB to carry out its consumer-protection duties.

for.name: 5 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Reps. Carolyn Maloney, Wm. Lacy Clay, Al Green, Gwen Moore, and Emanuel Cleaver.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it never received a markup or vote in committee.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor before the Congress ended.

against.name: Mick Mulvaney
against.role: Acting Director, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
against.what_they_did: Served as the acting head of the CFPB whose policies the bill was written to reverse; he had dropped payday-lender lawsuits, stopped penalty-fund payments to harmed consumers, and scaled back the agency's fair-lending and student-lending offices.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled House; there is no recorded floor vote showing the exact split.

industries.industry: Banks, payday lenders, and debt collectors
industries.note: These firms are the CFPB's main enforcement targets; the bill restores staff, supervision, and enforcement the agency had scaled back in 2018. Their savings from weaker oversight came at the expense of consumers facing fees, discrimination, and abusive collection.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and banks on campuses
industries.note: The bill recreates a dedicated student-lending office and ombudsman and orders an inquiry into whether leadership suppressed a report on banks charging students account fees. Servicers would face renewed scrutiny.

The bill caps the number of political appointees and prevents directors from renaming or dismantling statutorily created offices, trading director flexibility for continuity of the agency's consumer mission.
